title: The Sadducees’ Court
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman writes: Throughout the Sanhedrin’s existence, from the day Ezra came up from the exile until the destruction of the Temple, the whole Sanhedrin was always made up of the pious and the great of Israel—except in the old age of Yochanan the High Priest, who became a Sadducee and turned into a hater of the Pharisees. Then the Sanhedrin belonged to the Sadducee sect, until Shimon ben Shetach came and, with his great wisdom, drove them out one by one, for he showed everyone that they were ignorant and unlearned. And the second occasion was before the destruction, when the wicked high priests joined together; because of them the Temple was destroyed and Israel was exiled from its land. Had the Lord not raised up for us a deliverer, R’ Yochanan ben Zakkai (רי״בז), there would have been—Heaven forbid—annihilation of the entire people. I have already discussed this at length in the entries on Shimon ben Shetach and רא״ברצ.

notes.text: The cross-reference רא״ברצ remains unresolved. The account of the Sadducees, high priests and rescue of the people is Hyman’s strongly worded historical argument, not a new historical adjudication.

The whole account is Hyman’s strongly worded historical argument: always, the exception in Yochanan’s old age, expulsion one by one, the second occasion before destruction, wicked high priests, destruction and exile because of them, and the counterfactual annihilation are preserved without a new historical adjudication. Yochanan the High Priest is not independently identified as Hyrcanus. The conventional contextual name expansion of רי״בז is Yochanan ben Zakkai, but the abbreviated title remains R-prime; full Rabban is not supplied by this passage or a newly read exact witness. The final רא״ברצ remains an unresolved entry cross-reference. Its possible expansion is not adopted, and no roster, person or authority identity is admitted. All source holds remain.

Hyman’s entry on Shimon ben Shetach (vol. III, pp. 1212–1213) quotes the scholion to Megillat Ta’anit for 28 Tevet. The scholion describes Shimon replacing members one at a time after challenging them to support their rulings from the Torah. Hyman’s discussion under Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok (vol. I, p. 203) uses the same abbreviation רא״ברצ and supplies the corresponding account. There Hyman discusses the account in Sanhedrin 52b, where Rav Yosef identifies a Sadducee court and the Gemara distinguishes two incidents. The consulted sources supply these local parallels. The two-period account and its causal and counterfactual claims are Hyman’s historical argument.
